claim: Nucleation promoting factors (NPFs) initiate branched actin network assembly by activating Arp2/3 complex.
source: Nucleation promoting factors (NPFs) initiate branched actin network assembly by activating Arp2/3 complex, a branched actin filament nucleator.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about NPFs and Arp2/3 complex function.

claim: Arp2/3 complex is a branched actin filament nucleator.
source: Nucleation promoting factors (NPFs) initiate branched actin network assembly by activating Arp2/3 complex, a branched actin filament nucleator.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of Arp2/3 complex.

claim: Cellular actin networks contain multiple NPFs.
source: Cellular actin networks contain multiple NPFs, but how they coordinately regulate Arp2/3 complex is unclear.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the composition of cellular actin networks.

claim: How multiple NPFs coordinately regulate Arp2/3 complex is unclear.
source: Cellular actin networks contain multiple NPFs, but how they coordinately regulate Arp2/3 complex is unclear.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current scientific understanding.

claim: Cortactin is an NPF that activates Arp2/3 complex weakly on its own.
source: Cortactin is an NPF that activates Arp2/3 complex weakly on its own, but with WASP/N-WASP, another class of NPFs, potently activates.
evidence: This is supported by prior literature and experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Cortactin with WASP/N-WASP potently activates Arp2/3 complex.
source: Cortactin is an NPF that activates Arp2/3 complex weakly on its own, but with WASP/N-WASP, another class of NPFs, potently activates.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript showing synergistic activation.

claim: Cortactin displaces N-WASP from nascent branches as a prerequisite for nucleation.
source: We dissect the mechanism of synergy and propose a model in which cortactin displaces N-WASP from nascent branches as a prerequisite for nucleation.
evidence: This is the main model proposed based on experimental data and mathematical modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: Unlike WASP/N-WASP, cortactin remains bound to junctions during nucleation.
source: Single-molecule imaging revealed that unlike WASP/N-WASP, cortactin remains bound to junctions during nucleation, and specifically targets junctions with a ∼160-fold increased on rate over filament sides.
evidence: This is supported by single-molecule TIRF microscopy data shown in the manuscript.

claim: Cortactin specifically targets junctions with a ∼160-fold increased on rate over filament sides.
source: Single-molecule imaging revealed that unlike WASP/N-WASP, cortactin remains bound to junctions during nucleation, and specifically targets junctions with a ∼160-fold increased on rate over filament sides.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of single-molecule binding kinetics presented in Figure 7.

claim: N-WASP must be dimerized for potent synergy.
source: N-WASP must be dimerized for potent synergy, and targeted mutations indicate release of dimeric N-WASP from nascent branches limits nucleation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing monomeric and dimeric N-WASP constructs shown in Figure 4.

claim: Release of dimeric N-WASP from nascent branches limits nucleation.
source: N-WASP must be dimerized for potent synergy, and targeted mutations indicate release of dimeric N-WASP from nascent branches limits nucleation.
evidence: This is supported by mutational analysis data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Cortactin-mediated displacement but not N-WASP recycling or filament recruitment models can explain synergy.
source: Mathematical modeling shows cortactin-mediated displacement but not N-WASP recycling or filament recruitment models can explain synergy.
evidence: This is supported by mathematical modeling results presented in Figures 3 and 9.

claim: Arp2/3 complex mediates the assembly of branched actin filament networks by nucleating new (daughter) filaments from the sides of pre-existing (mother) filaments.
source: Actin-related protein (Arp)-2/3 complex is an important actin cytoskeletal regulator that mediates the assembly of branched actin filament networks by nucleating new (daughter) filaments from the sides of pre-existing (mother) filaments (Figure 1A) (Goley and Welch, 2006; Rotty et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: When isolated from most species, Arp2/3 complex is inactive.
source: When isolated from most species, the complex is inactive, and activation requires binding to the side of a preformed actin filament and association with a nucleation promoting factor (NPF) protein (Figure 1A) (Pollard, 2007; Achard et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Activation of Arp2/3 complex requires binding to the side of a preformed actin filament and association with a nucleation promoting factor (NPF) protein.
source: When isolated from most species, the complex is inactive, and activation requires binding to the side of a preformed actin filament and association with a nucleation promoting factor (NPF) protein (Figure 1A) (Pollard, 2007; Achard et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Type I NPFs bind actin monomers.
source: In addition to binding Arp2/3 complex, NPFs discovered to date bind either actin monomers (type I NPFs) or filaments (type II NPFs) (Goley and Welch, 2006) (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Type II NPFs bind actin filaments.
source: In addition to binding Arp2/3 complex, NPFs discovered to date bind either actin monomers (type I NPFs) or filaments (type II NPFs) (Goley and Welch, 2006) (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Cellular branched actin structures contain multiple NPFs, including representatives from both classes.
source: Cellular branched actin structures contain multiple NPFs, including representatives from both classes, which frequently have non-redundant roles in actin network assembly (Galletta et al., 2008; Yamaguchi et al., 2005; Ayala et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Multiple NPFs in cellular branched actin structures frequently have non-redundant roles in actin network assembly.
source: Cellular branched actin structures contain multiple NPFs, including representatives from both classes, which frequently have non-redundant roles in actin network assembly (Galletta et al., 2008; Yamaguchi et al., 2005; Ayala et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The mechanism by which multiple NPFs coordinately regulate Arp2/3 complex activity is poorly understood.
source: However, the mechanism by which multiple NPFs coordinately regulate Arp2/3 complex activity is poorly understood.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current scientific understanding.

claim: WASP and Scar family proteins are the best studied type I NPFs.
source: WASP (Wiskot-Aldrich syndrome) and Scar (suppressor of cAR) family proteins, the best studied type I NPFs, have a minimal Arp2/3-activation region called VCA (verprolin homology, central, acidic, Figure 1B) (Goley and Welch, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: WASP and Scar family proteins have a minimal Arp2/3-activation region called VCA.
source: WASP (Wiskot-Aldrich syndrome) and Scar (suppressor of cAR) family proteins, the best studied type I NPFs, have a minimal Arp2/3-activation region called VCA (verprolin homology, central, acidic, Figure 1B) (Goley and Welch, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The V and C regions of VCA bind actin monomers.
source: The V and C regions of VCA bind actin monomers (Kelly et al., 2006), and CA binds two sites on Arp2/3 complex (Padrick et al., 2011; Ti et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: CA binds two sites on Arp2/3 complex.
source: The V and C regions of VCA bind actin monomers (Kelly et al., 2006), and CA binds two sites on Arp2/3 complex (Padrick et al., 2011; Ti et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: One CA binding site is on Arp3 and the other spans Arp2 and ARPC1.
source: Chemical crosslinking assays demonstrate that one CA site is on Arp3 and the other spans Arp2 and ARPC1 (Padrick et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: VCA recruits actin monomers to the Arp2 and Arp3 subunits, stimulating a conformational rearrangement to create an Arp2-Arp3-actin hetero-oligomer that mimics a stable actin filament nucleus.
source: Using two CA binding sites, VCA is thought to recruit actin monomers to the Arp2 and Arp3 subunits, stimulating a conformational rearrangement to create an Arp2-Arp3-actin hetero-oligomer that mimics a stable actin filament nucleus (Padrick et al., 2011; Hetrick et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a mechanistic model supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Monomeric vs oligomeric VCA regions activate Arp2/3 complex with distinct kinetics.
source: Monomeric vs oligomeric VCA regions activate the complex with distinct kinetics, presumably due to differential engagement of the two sites (Padrick et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Oligomerization of WASP/Scar proteins is thought to tune NPF activity in vivo.
source: Oligomerization of WASP/Scar proteins is thought to tune NPF activity in vivo (Padrick et al., 2008; Gohl et al., 2010; Footer et al., 2008), so dissecting biochemical differences between monomeric and oligomeric NPFs is an important challenge.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cortactin was initially discovered as a Src kinase substrate and actin binding protein.
source: Cortactin, the prototypical type II NPF, was initially discovered as a Src kinase substrate and actin binding protein (Wu and Parsons, 1993), and was later found to directly bind and activate Arp2/3 complex (Weed et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cortactin was later found to directly bind and activate Arp2/3 complex.
source: Cortactin, the prototypical type II NPF, was initially discovered as a Src kinase substrate and actin binding protein (Wu and Parsons, 1993), and was later found to directly bind and activate Arp2/3 complex (Weed et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Cortactin contains an N-terminal acidic region (NtA), which interacts with Arp2/3 complex.
source: Cortactin contains an N-terminal acidic region (NtA), which interacts with Arp2/3 complex, 6.5 actin filament binding repeat sequences, and a C-terminal SH3 domain (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the domain structure of cortactin.

claim: Cortactin contains 6.5 actin filament binding repeat sequences.
source: Cortactin contains an N-terminal acidic region (NtA), which interacts with Arp2/3 complex, 6.5 actin filament binding repeat sequences, and a C-terminal SH3 domain (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the domain structure of cortactin.

claim: Cortactin contains a C-terminal SH3 domain.
source: Cortactin contains an N-terminal acidic region (NtA), which interacts with Arp2/3 complex, 6.5 actin filament binding repeat sequences, and a C-terminal SH3 domain (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the domain structure of cortactin.

claim: Mutations in the NtA that block its interaction with Arp2/3 complex prevent assembly of actin in invadopodia.
source: Mutations in the NtA that block its interaction with Arp2/3 complex prevent assembly of actin in protrusive structures in transformed cells called invadopodia, and hinder actin-dependent vesicle trafficking required for lamellipodial protrusion and cellular motility (Bryce et al., 2005; Ayala et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mutations in the NtA that block its interaction with Arp2/3 complex hinder actin-dependent vesicle trafficking required for lamellipodial protrusion and cellular motility.
source: Mutations in the NtA that block its interaction with Arp2/3 complex prevent assembly of actin in protrusive structures in transformed cells called invadopodia, and hinder actin-dependent vesicle trafficking required for lamellipodial protrusion and cellular motility (Bryce et al., 2005; Ayala et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cortactin plays an important role in regulating Arp2/3 complex in vivo.
source: These observations demonstrate that cortactin plays an important role in regulating Arp2/3 complex in vivo, yet the precise mechanism of Arp2/3 complex activation is unclear.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited mutational studies showing functional consequences.

claim: The precise mechanism of Arp2/3 complex activation by cortactin is unclear.
source: These observations demonstrate that cortactin plays an important role in regulating Arp2/3 complex in vivo, yet the precise mechanism of Arp2/3 complex activation is unclear.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current scientific understanding.

claim: The actin filament-binding repeats of cortactin are required for activation.
source: Because the actin filament-binding repeats are required for activation, it has been hypothesized that cortactin recruits Arp2/3 complex to filaments to stimulate nucleation (Uruno et al., 2001) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: It has been hypothesized that cortactin recruits Arp2/3 complex to filaments to stimulate nucleation.
source: Because the actin filament-binding repeats are required for activation, it has been hypothesized that cortactin recruits Arp2/3 complex to filaments to stimulate nucleation (Uruno et al., 2001) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior literature supported by citation.

claim: Whether filament recruitment can explain the acceleration of branching nucleation is unknown.
source: However, whether filament recruitment can explain the acceleration of branching nucleation is unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current scientific understanding.

claim: Cortactin on its own is a weak activator of Arp2/3 complex in vitro.
source: In addition, cortactin on its own is a weak activator of Arp2/3 complex in vitro (Weed et al., 2000), making it uncertain how cortactin can contribute to branching nucleation in vivo.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: In the presence of WASP/Scar proteins, cortactin potently activates Arp2/3 complex.
source: Importantly, in the presence of WASP/Scar proteins, cortactin potently activates Arp2/3 complex (Weaver et al., 2001; Uruno et al., 2001), suggesting these NPFs synergize to assemble branched actin structures in vivo (see Figure 1C for schematic).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: WASP/Scar proteins and cortactin synergize to assemble branched actin structures in vivo.
source: Importantly, in the presence of WASP/Scar proteins, cortactin potently activates Arp2/3 complex (Weaver et al., 2001; Uruno et al., 2001), suggesting these NPFs synergize to assemble branched actin structures in vivo (see Figure 1C for schematic).
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the observation of synergistic activation in vitro.

claim: WASP/Scar proteins and cortactin co-localize in many branched networks in vivo, including at the leading edge of motile cells, podosomes and invadopodia, and at sites of endocytosis.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, WASP/Scar proteins and cortactin co-localize in many branched networks in vivo, including at the leading edge of motile cells, podosomes and invadopodia, and at sites of endocytosis (Martinez-Quiles et al., 2004; DesMarais et al., 2009; Grassart et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: N-WASP and cortactin compete for binding to Arp3.
source: Previous data showed that N-WASP and cortactin compete for binding to Arp3 (Weaver et al., 2002), and cortactin competes more strongly when Arp2/3 complex is bound to filaments (Uruno et al., 2003), but the precise mechanism of synergy is unknown.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Cortactin competes more strongly for binding to Arp3 when Arp2/3 complex is bound to filaments.
source: Previous data showed that N-WASP and cortactin compete for binding to Arp3 (Weaver et al., 2002), and cortactin competes more strongly when Arp2/3 complex is bound to filaments (Uruno et al., 2003), but the precise mechanism of synergy is unknown.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The precise mechanism of synergy between N-WASP and cortactin is unknown.
source: Previous data showed that N-WASP and cortactin compete for binding to Arp3 (Weaver et al., 2002), and cortactin competes more strongly when Arp2/3 complex is bound to filaments (Uruno et al., 2003), but the precise mechanism of synergy is unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current scientific understanding.

claim: Cortactin dramatically increased the polymerization rate in reactions with GST-N-WASP-VCA and Arp2/3 complex.
source: Cortactin dramatically increased the polymerization rate, and the concentration dependence of synergy followed a hyperbolic trend (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: The concentration dependence of cortactin-mediated synergy followed a hyperbolic trend.
source: Cortactin dramatically increased the polymerization rate, and the concentration dependence of synergy followed a hyperbolic trend (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The concentration of cortactin required for half-maximal synergy was 72 nM.
source: The concentration of cortactin required for half-maximal synergy was 72 nM and saturating cortactin increased the maximum polymerization rate 3.5–3.8-fold over GST-VCA alone.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from fitting experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Saturating cortactin increased the maximum polymerization rate 3.5–3.8-fold over GST-VCA alone.
source: The concentration of cortactin required for half-maximal synergy was 72 nM and saturating cortactin increased the maximum polymerization rate 3.5–3.8-fold over GST-VCA alone.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Cortactin did not inhibit Arp2/3 complex at any concentration tested, up to 20 μM in pyrene actin polymerization assays or 1 μM in TIRF microscopy branching assays.
source: In contrast to a previous report, cortactin did not inhibit Arp2/3 complex at any concentration we tested, up to 20 μM in pyrene actin polymerization assays or 1 μM in TIRF microscopy branching assays (Siton et al., 2011) (Figure 1B–D and Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2B-D and Video 1.

claim: Cortactin might synergize with GST-VCA by recruiting Arp2/3 complex to actin filament sides.
source: Several lines of evidence suggest cortactin might synergize with GST-VCA by recruiting Arp2/3 complex to actin filament sides.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on multiple lines of evidence discussed in the text.

claim: Arp2/3 complex must bind to the side of a pre-existing filament to be activated.
source: First, Arp2/3 complex must bind to the side of a pre-existing filament to be activated (Achard et al., 2010), and kinetic measurements of pyrene-labeled S. pombe Arp2/3 complex indicated this binding step is slow (Beltzner and Pollard, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Kinetic measurements of pyrene-labeled S. pombe Arp2/3 complex indicated the filament binding step is slow.
source: First, Arp2/3 complex must bind to the side of a pre-existing filament to be activated (Achard et al., 2010), and kinetic measurements of pyrene-labeled S. pombe Arp2/3 complex indicated this binding step is slow (Beltzner and Pollard, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Deletion of the actin filament binding domain of cortactin abolished its weak intrinsic nucleation activity.
source: Second, deletion of the actin filament binding domain of cortactin abolished its weak intrinsic nucleation activity (Uruno et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Cortactin increases copelleting of Arp2/3 complex with actin filaments.
source: Finally, cortactin increases copelleting of Arp2/3 complex with actin filaments (Cai et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The mathematical model of branching nucleation in the presence of GST-VCA and Arp2/3 complex without cortactin fit the experimental data well.
source: The model fit the experimental data well, showing a good visual fit to the time courses and a low residual sum of squares (1.3 × 10−11) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The optimized value for knuc is 0.0038 s−1.
source: We fixed the on rate at 1.4 × 106 M−1 s−1 based on modeling of reactions containing cortactin (see below and 'Materials and methods'), and determined the optimized value for knuc is 0.0038 s−1.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from mathematical modeling.

claim: The optimized knuc value is 320-fold smaller than the calculated off rate of the nascent branch complex from filament sides.
source: This value is 320-fold smaller than the calculated off rate of the nascent branch complex from filament sides, consistent with smTIRF studies that show Arp2/3 complex binds and is released from filaments many times before nucleating a branch (Smith et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of modeling results with prior experimental observations.

claim: smTIRF studies show Arp2/3 complex binds and is released from filaments many times before nucleating a branch.
source: This value is 320-fold smaller than the calculated off rate of the nascent branch complex from filament sides, consistent with smTIRF studies that show Arp2/3 complex binds and is released from filaments many times before nucleating a branch (Smith et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Increasing side binding sites increased the polymerization rate, but could not account for the dramatic rate increases observed in experiments containing cortactin.
source: Using kfil_on determined from the experimental data with cortactin (1.4 × 106 M−1 s−1, see below, blue line in Figure 3C), we found that increasing side binding sites increased the polymerization rate, but could not account for the dramatic rate increases we observed in experiments containing cortactin (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by mathematical modeling results shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Filament recruitment cannot account for cortactin-mediated synergy.
source: This suggests that filament recruitment cannot account for cortactin-mediated synergy.
evidence: This is inferred from the mathematical modeling results.

claim: NtA was synergistic with GST-VCA, demonstrating that actin filament binding is not required for synergy.
source: We found NtA was synergistic with GST-VCA, demonstrating that actin filament binding is not required for synergy (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The concentration of NtA required for half-maximal synergy was 11 µM, 110-fold higher than for full-length cortactin.
source: The concentration dependence of synergy for both constructs followed a hyperbolic trend, and the concentration of NtA required for half-maximal synergy was 11 µM, 110-fold higher than for full-length cortactin.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: At saturation, NtA was as potent as full-length cortactin, increasing the maximum polymerization rate 3.8-fold over GST-VCA-mediated activation of Arp2/3 complex.
source: However, at saturation, NtA was as potent as full-length cortactin, increasing the maximum polymerization rate 3.8-fold over GST-VCA-mediated activation of Arp2/3 complex.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The NtA is sufficient for synergy, but the actin filament binding repeats allow cortactin to synergize at lower concentrations.
source: These data demonstrate that the NtA is sufficient for synergy, but that the actin filament binding repeats allow cortactin to synergize at lower concentrations.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data comparing full-length cortactin and NtA.

claim: Dimerization of VCA increases its binding affinity for Arp2/3 complex.
source: Dimerization of VCA is known to increase its binding affinity for Arp2/3 complex, and some evidence suggests WASP/Scar proteins function as oligomers in vivo (Padrick et al., 2008; Gohl et al., 2010; Footer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Some evidence suggests WASP/Scar proteins function as oligomers in vivo.
source: Dimerization of VCA is known to increase its binding affinity for Arp2/3 complex, and some evidence suggests WASP/Scar proteins function as oligomers in vivo (Padrick et al., 2008; Gohl et al., 2010; Footer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: GST-VCA behaved similarly to WASP dimerized through physiological SH3-polyproline interactions.
source: In previous experiments, GST-VCA behaved similarly to WASP dimerized through physiological SH3-polyproline interactions, so artificial dimerization by GST can mimic in vivo dimerization mechanisms (Padrick et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Saturating cortactin enhanced the maximum polymerization rate of a reaction containing GST-VCA 3.7-fold over the rate without cortactin.
source: Saturating cortactin enhanced the maximum polymerization rate of a reaction containing GST-VCA 3.7-fold over the rate without cortactin, whereas cortactin weakly influenced a reaction containing monomeric VCA, accelerating the reaction only ∼1.5-fold over VCA alone (Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: Cortactin weakly influenced a reaction containing monomeric VCA, accelerating the reaction only ∼1.5-fold over VCA alone.
source: Saturating cortactin enhanced the maximum polymerization rate of a reaction containing GST-VCA 3.7-fold over the rate without cortactin, whereas cortactin weakly influenced a reaction containing monomeric VCA, accelerating the reaction only ∼1.5-fold over VCA alone (Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: Increasing the concentration of monomeric VCA did not increase synergy.
source: Increasing the concentration of monomeric VCA did not increase synergy, suggesting the failure to observe potent synergy is not due to under-saturation of two CA binding sites on the complex (Figure 4B,C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: VCA dimerized with a leucine zipper (LZ-VCA) behaved identically to GST-VCA.
source: VCA dimerized with a leucine zipper (LZ-VCA) behaved identically to GST-VCA, demonstrating that the difference in synergy is due to the oligomerization state of the VCA rather than an artifact caused by GST (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The difference in synergy between monomeric and dimeric VCA is due to the oligomerization state of the VCA rather than an artifact caused by GST.
source: VCA dimerized with a leucine zipper (LZ-VCA) behaved identically to GST-VCA, demonstrating that the difference in synergy is due to the oligomerization state of the VCA rather than an artifact caused by GST (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data comparing GST-VCA and LZ-VCA.

claim: VVCA is not synergistic with cortactin at any concentration.
source: We found that VVCA is not synergistic with cortactin at any concentration (Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: The ability to recruit two actin monomers to the complex using one NPF binding site is not sufficient for synergy.
source: These data suggest that the ability to recruit two actin monomers to the complex using one NPF binding site is not sufficient for synergy.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing VVCA is not synergistic with cortactin.

claim: Type I NPF release is required for nucleation.
source: Based on a number of observations, we hypothesized that type I NPF release is required for nucleation, and that tight binding of the type I NPF can slow the final activation step.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on multiple observations discussed in the text.

claim: At saturation, VCA is a better activator of Arp2/3 complex than GST-VCA.
source: First, we observed that at saturation, VCA is a better activator of Arp2/3 complex than GST-VCA (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Recent single-molecule imaging experiments show that WASP dissociates from the branch junctions before elongation of the daughter filament.
source: Second, recent single-molecule imaging experiments show that WASP dissociates from the branch junctions before elongation of the daughter filament (Martin et al., 2006) (Smith et al., 2013, in press at eLife).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Crystal structures show that the V region may block the barbed end of actin monomers, preventing interactions with incoming actin monomers required for elongation.
source: Finally, crystal structures show that the V region may block the barbed end of actin monomers, preventing interactions with incoming actin monomers required for elongation (Chereau et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Cortactin synergizes with GST-VCA by displacing it from the nascent branch complex, increasing the rate of the final activation step by accelerating the obligatory release of GST-VCA.
source: Therefore, we hypothesized that cortactin synergizes with GST-VCA by displacing it from the nascent branch complex, increasing the rate of the final activation step by accelerating the obligatory release of GST-VCA (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on multiple observations and is the main model proposed in the manuscript.

claim: The R442A mutation in VCA decreased its affinity for actin monomers 20-fold.
source: To test this model, we prepared a VCA construct (GST-VCA(R442A)) with a point mutation in V that decreases its affinity for actin monomers 20-fold (Co et al., 2007) (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and citation to prior literature.

claim: The maximal polymerization rate at saturation was increased 2.5-fold in the R442A mutant compared to wild type.
source: Consistent with this prediction, the maximal polymerization rate at saturation was increased 2.5-fold in the R442A mutant compared to wild type (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In the presence of the R442A mutant, cortactin showed approximately twofold less synergy compared to the wild-type GST-VCA.
source: In the presence of the R442A mutant, cortactin showed approximately twofold less synergy compared to the wild-type GST-VCA (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The E455R mutation had no influence on the affinity of N-WASP-VCA for actin monomers.
source: Interestingly, this mutation had no influence on the affinity of N-WASP-VCA for actin monomers (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The E455R mutation decreased the maximal polymerization rate at saturation.
source: However, it decreased the maximal polymerization rate at saturation (Figure 5A) and increased synergy with cortactin (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The E455R mutation increased synergy with cortactin.
source: However, it decreased the maximal polymerization rate at saturation (Figure 5A) and increased synergy with cortactin (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The E455R/E93 interaction may occur only in the context of the nascent branch junction.
source: This suggests that the E455R/E93 interaction may occur only in the context of the nascent branch junction.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that E455R does not affect actin monomer binding but does affect nucleation kinetics.

claim: The actin filament-binding region of cortactin is composed of 6.5 tandem 37-amino acid repeats, which are unstructured.
source: The actin filament-binding region of cortactin is composed of 6.5 tandem 37-amino acid repeats, which are unstructured (Shvetsov et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Single-molecules of cortactin bound to and dissociated from actin filaments during the time courses of the videos.
source: Single-molecules of cortactin bound to and dissociated from actin filaments during the time courses of the videos (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by single-molecule TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 6A and Video 2.

claim: Cortactin molecules bound statically to actin filaments.
source: The cortactin molecules bound statically, eliminating the possibility that cortactin targets nascent branch junctions by diffusing along filaments (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by single-molecule TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The off rate of cortactin from actin filament sides is 0.050 s−1.
source: We measured the lifetimes of bound cortactin molecules and fit the cumulative lifetime data to a single exponential decay equation and determined an off rate (koff) of 0.050 s−1 (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from single-molecule TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Cortactin bound to both filament sides and branch junctions when added to a TIRF chamber with preformed branches.
source: Cortactin added to a TIRF chamber with preformed branches bound to both filament sides and branch junctions (Figure 7A, Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by single-molecule TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 7A and Video 3.

claim: The off rate of cortactin for branch junctions was 0.034 s−1, almost twofold slower than the off rate for preformed filament sides measured from the same reaction (0.063 s−1).
source: The off rate of cortactin for branch junctions was 0.034 s−1, almost twofold slower than the off rate for preformed filament sides measured from the same reaction (0.063 s−1) (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from single-molecule TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: 30% of the 270 tracked cortactin molecules were bound to branch junctions even though branches made up only ∼0.13% of total cortactin binding sites.
source: Interestingly, 30% of the 270 tracked cortactin molecules were bound to branch junctions even though branches made up only ∼0.13% (68 branch junctions vs ∼53,000 filament side binding sites) of total cortactin binding sites (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from single-molecule TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 7C and 7D.

claim: Cortactin binds with a significantly higher affinity to branch junctions than filament sides.
source: This suggests that cortactin binds with a significantly higher affinity to branch junctions than filament sides.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cortactin preferentially binds to branch junctions despite their low abundance.

claim: The affinity of cortactin for branch junctions is ∼300-fold greater than for filament sides: 17 nM vs 5.2 µM, respectively.
source: Using the average fraction bound, we determined that the affinity of cortactin for branch junctions is ∼300-fold greater than for filament sides: 17 nM vs 5.2 µM, respectively (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from analysis of single-molecule TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The calculated on rates of cortactin for branch junctions and filament sides are 2.0 × 106 M−1 s−1 and 1.2 × 104 M−1 s−1, respectively.
source: Using these equilibrium constants and our previously measured off rates, the calculated on rates of cortactin for branch junctions and filament sides are 2.0 × 106 M−1 s−1 and 1.2 × 104 M−1 s−1, respectively.
evidence: This is calculated from measured equilibrium constants and off rates.

claim: Cortactin targets branch junctions by binding over two orders of magnitude more tightly to junctions than filament sides.
source: Our data show that cortactin targets branch junctions by binding over two orders of magnitude more tightly to junctions than filament sides.
evidence: This is inferred from the quantitative binding kinetics measurements.

claim: High affinity binding to branch junctions is accomplished through a ∼160-fold increase in the on rate and further amplified by a ∼twofold decrease in the off rate.
source: High affinity binding to branch junctions is accomplished through a ∼160-fold increase in the on rate and further amplified by a ∼twofold decrease in the off rate.
evidence: This is inferred from the quantitative binding kinetics measurements.

claim: Multiple instances (n = 66) were observed in which cortactin bound to the side of a filament where a daughter filament was later nucleated.
source: We observed multiple instances (n = 66) in which cortactin bound to the side of a filament where a daughter filament was later nucleated (Figure 8A,B, Videos 4 and 5).
evidence: This is supported by single-molecule TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 8A and 8B.

claim: In each instance, cortactin remained bound to the branch junction after nucleation.
source: In each instance, cortactin remained bound to the branch junction after nucleation, consistent with the predictions of the obligatory displacement model.
evidence: This is supported by single-molecule TIRF microscopy data.

claim: The average lifetime of cortactin at the junction after nucleation was 62 s, 2.1-fold longer than the average lifetime of cortactin binding to a preformed branch junction.
source: The average lifetime at the junction after nucleation was 62 s, 2.1-fold longer than the average lifetime of cortactin binding to a preformed branch junction (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from single-molecule TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The average lifetime of cortactin before nucleation was 6.5 s.
source: The average lifetime before nucleation was 6.5 s.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from single-molecule TIRF microscopy data.

claim: During active branching, cortactin bound existing branch junctions with an average lifetime of 29.5 s, the same lifetime found using preformed filament reactions (29.1 s).
source: During active branching, cortactin bound existing branch junctions with an average lifetime of 29.5 s, the same lifetime found using preformed filament reactions (29.1 s).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from single-molecule TIRF microscopy data.

claim: The lifetime of cortactin molecules on filament sides during active branching was 2.0–2.5-fold lower (8.0 s) than with preformed filaments or polymerizing filaments in the absence of Arp2/3 complex.
source: Interestingly, the lifetime of cortactin molecules on filament sides was 2.0–2.5-fold lower (8.0 s) than with preformed filaments or polymerizing filaments in the absence of Arp2/3 complex.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from single-molecule TIRF microscopy data.

claim: Single-molecules of NtA were observed bound to existing branch junctions and to nascent branches from which new daughter filaments nucleated.
source: Single-molecules of NtA were observed bound to existing branch junctions and to nascent branches from which new daughter filaments nucleated (Figure 8C and Video 6).
evidence: This is supported by single-molecule TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 8C and Video 6.

claim: NtA can directly engage Arp2/3 complex after and during branch nucleation and does not block daughter filament elongation.
source: These data indicate that NtA can directly engage Arp2/3 complex after and during branch nucleation and that it does not block daughter filament elongation.
evidence: This is inferred from single-molecule TIRF microscopy observations.

claim: The obligatory displacement model fit the experimental data well.
source: This model fit the experimental data well (Figure 9B,C).
evidence: This is supported by mathematical modeling results shown in Figure 9B and 9C.

claim: The optimized value for displacement activation (kdis) was 0.036 s−1, 10-fold higher than the activation step in the absence of cortactin, knuc.
source: Above the threshold, the optimized value for displacement activation (kdis) was 0.036 s−1, 10-fold higher than the activation step in the absence of cortactin, knuc (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from mathematical modeling shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The kinetic pathway of the obligatory displacement model fits the experimental data well, indicating that this model can explain synergy.
source: Nevertheless, the kinetic pathway of the obligatory displacement model fits the experimental data well, indicating that this model can explain synergy.
evidence: This is inferred from the mathematical modeling results.

claim: The recycling displacement model could not fit the data because increasing concentrations of cortactin had no influence on modeled polymerization rates.
source: The recycling displacement model could not fit the data because increasing concentrations of cortactin had no influence on modeled polymerization rates.
evidence: This is supported by mathematical modeling results.

claim: In the absence of cortactin, only 3.8% of the total GST-VCA was sequestered at the end of the reaction.
source: In the absence of cortactin, only 3.8% of the total GST-VCA was sequestered at the end of the reaction (Figure 9E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from mathematical modeling shown in Figure 9E.

claim: The recycling model cannot account for the synergistic activation of Arp2/3 complex observed in the assays.
source: Therefore, the recycling model cannot account for the synergistic activation of Arp2/3 complex we observe in our assays.
evidence: This is inferred from the mathematical modeling results showing the recycling model cannot fit the data.

claim: In the obligatory displacement model, GST-VCA, two actin monomers and Arp2/3 complex assemble on the side of a filament, creating a nascent branch junction.
source: In this model, GST-VCA, two actin monomers and Arp2/3 complex assemble on the side of a filament, creating a nascent branch junction.
evidence: This is a description of the proposed obligatory displacement model.

claim: Cortactin targets the nascent branch junction, making a multivalent interaction with Arp2/3 complex and the adjacent mother filament.
source: Cortactin targets the junction, making a multivalent interaction with Arp2/3 complex and the adjacent mother filament.
evidence: This is a description of the proposed obligatory displacement model.

claim: At the nascent branch junction, NtA can compete with CA at the Arp3 binding site on the complex.
source: At the nascent branch junction, NtA can compete with CA at the Arp3 binding site on the complex, as previously reported (Weaver et al., 2002; Padrick et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Release of one CA speeds release of the GST-VCA, allowing nucleation and elongation to proceed.
source: Release of one CA speeds release of the GST-VCA, allowing nucleation and elongation to proceed.
evidence: This is a description of the proposed obligatory displacement model.

claim: NtA does not block elongation.
source: Importantly, NtA does not block elongation, as we demonstrate by visualizing labeled NtA at nascent branch junctions during nucleation/elongation.
evidence: This is supported by single-molecule TIRF microscopy data.

claim: NtA stays engaged with Arp2/3 complex and the repeats stay bound to the mother filament after elongation, allowing cortactin to remain tightly bound to the mature branch junction.
source: Rather, NtA stays engaged with Arp2/3 complex and the repeats stay bound to the mother filament after elongation, allowing cortactin to remain tightly bound to the mature branch junction.
evidence: This is inferred from single-molecule TIRF microscopy observations.

claim: smTIRF measurements are consistent with immuno-gold-labeled electron micrographs and three-dimensional EM reconstructions that show cortactin remains at the mature branch junction.
source: Our smTIRF measurements are consistent with immuno-gold-labeled electron micrographs and three-dimensional EM reconstructions that show cortactin remains at the mature branch junction (Cai et al., 2008; Egile et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of the current data with prior literature.

claim: The obligatory displacement model is consistent with the observation that cortactin competes weakly with GST-VCA in the absence of filaments, but strongly in their presence.
source: The obligatory displacement model is also consistent with the observation that cortactin competes weakly with GST-VCA in the absence of filaments, but strongly in their presence (Uruno et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of the model with prior literature.

claim: A mutation in the V region that decreased its affinity for actin increased the rate of nucleation at saturating GST-VCA.
source: Our mutational analyses support this requirement, since a mutation in the V region that decreased its affinity for actin increased the rate of nucleation at saturating GST-VCA, suggesting weakened interactions with the nascent branch junction can increase nucleation rates.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Recent single-molecule TIRF experiments show that VCA release precedes elongation of the daughter filament.
source: Additional evidence comes from recent single-molecule TIRF experiments, which show that VCA release precedes elongation of the daughter filament (Martin et al., 2006) (Smith et al., 2013, in press at eLife).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Because WASP/Scar proteins are attached to membranes, incorporation of the release step into the nucleation mechanism ensures branches are not strongly tethered to the membrane as the growing actin network pushes outward on it.
source: One possibility is that because WASP/Scar proteins are attached to membranes (Higgs and Pollard, 2000), incorporation of the release step into the nucleation mechanism ensures branches are not strongly tethered to the membrane as the growing actin network pushes outward on it.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on established knowledge and the proposed model.

claim: Akin et al. showed that increasing transient connections between bead-immobilized NPFs and nascent branch junctions decreased bead motility.
source: In support of this hypothesis, Akin et al. showed that increasing transient connections between bead-immobilized NPFs and nascent branch junctions decreased bead motility (Akin and Mullins, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Cortactin could stimulate release of a membrane bound NPF from Arp2/3 complex to regulate network-substrate connections.
source: Our data suggest cortactin could stimulate release of a membrane bound NPF from Arp2/3 complex to regulate network-substrate connections, providing an additional mode by which cortactin can control the dynamics of branched actin networks.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental data and proposed model.

claim: Addition of cortactin to a solution of GST-VCA coated beads increased the bead motility to an extent unlikely to be accounted for simply by an increased nucleation rate.
source: Recent experiments showed that addition of cortactin to a solution of GST-VCA coated beads increased the bead motility to an extent unlikely to be accounted for simply by an increased nucleation rate (Siton et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Cortactin may stimulate branched network dynamics both by increasing nucleation rates and by preventing stalling caused by tight membrane-network attachments.
source: Therefore, cortactin may stimulate branched network dynamics both by increasing nucleation rates and by preventing stalling caused by tight membrane-network attachments.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental data and prior literature.

claim: The on rate of cortactin for filament sides (12,100 M−1 s−1) is 200–2000-fold slower than for most other actin filament binding proteins.
source: This on rate is 200–2000-fold slower than for most other actin filament binding proteins, and is unlikely to be diffusion limited (Kovács et al., 2004; De La Cruz et al., 1999; Wegner and Ruhnau, 1988).
evidence: This is a comparison of the measured on rate with values from prior literature.

claim: Binding of cortactin to filament sides may be slow because it requires a conformational change in filaments.
source: Binding may be slow because it requires a conformational change in filaments, in agreement with an electron microscopy reconstruction showing that cortactin binding widens the gap between protofilaments (Pant et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the measured kinetics and prior structural data.

claim: In the case of the NtA construct, synergy must occur completely through nascent branch targeting.
source: While these pathways can be inserted into the model, we note that in the case of the NtA construct, synergy must occur completely through nascent branch targeting, suggesting nascent branch targeting may be the dominant displacement pathway for the full-length protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing NtA is synergistic without actin filament binding repeats.

claim: The actin filament binding repeats of cortactin are not required for synergy.
source: We showed the actin filament binding repeats of cortactin are not required for synergy, eliminating an actin filament recruitment mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing NtA is synergistic.

claim: Saturating concentrations of NtA activated nucleation to the same extent as saturating full-length cortactin.
source: While it is possible that recruitment operates simultaneously with displacement in full-length cortactin, we observed that saturating concentrations of NtA activated nucleation to the same extent as saturating full-length cortactin, so there is no recruitment component of synergy that cannot be mimicked by NtA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Cortactin can weakly activate Arp2/3 complex on its own.
source: Importantly, cortactin can weakly activate Arp2/3 complex on its own (Weed et al., 2000), and in contrast to synergy, this intrinsic activity requires the filament binding repeats (Uruno et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The intrinsic activity of cortactin requires the filament binding repeats.
source: Importantly, cortactin can weakly activate Arp2/3 complex on its own (Weed et al., 2000), and in contrast to synergy, this intrinsic activity requires the filament binding repeats (Uruno et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Filament recruitment may explain the weak intrinsic activity of cortactin observed in vitro.
source: Therefore, filament recruitment may explain the weak intrinsic activity of cortactin observed in vitro.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental data and prior literature.

claim: Cortactin directly influences nucleation at nascent branch junctions.
source: Our data are inconsistent with a previously proposed recycling model of synergy, in which cortactin indirectly increases nucleation rates by recycling WASP sequestered at mature branch junctions, freeing it to activate Arp2/3 complex (Siton et al., 2011). Instead, our data indicate that cortactin directly influences nucleation at nascent branch junctions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and mathematical modeling.

claim: Cortactin has been shown to stabilize branch junctions in vitro.
source: In addition to activating Arp2/3 complex, cortactin has been shown to stabilize branch junctions in vitro (Weaver et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The average lifetime of cortactin at branch junctions was 29.2 s.
source: The average lifetime of cortactin at branch junctions was 29.2 s, whereas the lifetime of branches has been reported to be between 8 and 27 min (Martin et al., 2006; Mahaffy and Pollard, 2006).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from single-molecule TIRF microscopy data.

claim: The lifetime of branches has been reported to be between 8 and 27 min.
source: The average lifetime of cortactin at branch junctions was 29.2 s, whereas the lifetime of branches has been reported to be between 8 and 27 min (Martin et al., 2006; Mahaffy and Pollard, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cortactin dissociates from branches much more rapidly than branches disassemble.
source: Given these data, cortactin dissociates from branches much more rapidly than branches disassemble.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing cortactin lifetime with branch lifetime.

claim: Cortactin has a high affinity for junctions (KD = 17 nM), so it likely dissociates and rebinds branches many times during the life of a branch.
source: However, cortactin has a high affinity for junctions (KD = 17 nM), so it likely dissociates and rebinds branches many times during the life of a branch, even when present at low (nanomolar) concentrations.
evidence: This is inferred from the measured affinity and lifetime data.

claim: Cortactin dynamically stabilizes branch junctions.
source: Therefore, cortactin dynamically stabilizes branch junctions.
evidence: This is inferred from the binding kinetics and affinity data.

claim: FRAP experiments show cortactin is incorporated into treadmilling networks not just at the leading edge but also throughout the entire network, and exchanges rapidly.
source: This mechanism is consistent with FRAP experiments that show cortactin is incorporated into treadmilling networks not just at the leading edge but also throughout the entire network, and exchanges rapidly (Lai et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: In vivo treadmilling networks turn over on much shorter timescales than in vitro branch lifetimes.
source: Importantly, in vivo treadmilling networks turn over on much shorter timescales than in vitro branch lifetimes (Lai et al., 2008; Martin et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In cells, the competition of cortactin with branch disassembly factors like GMF, coronin1B, and cofilin may be more important than the intrinsic branch stabilizing activity of cortactin.
source: In cells, the competition of cortactin with branch disassembly factors like GMF, coronin1B, and cofilin may be more important than the intrinsic branch stabilizing activity of cortactin (Gandhi et al., 2010; Cai et al., 2008; Blanchoin et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental data and prior literature.
